Deep-Guard Demo Runbook
Deep-Guard demo Why How it works At home In class The demo Future Questions If it breaks Words

Deep-Guard · demo runbook · Stage 4

Show Deep-Guard to anyone, from a fresh GitHub copy to a room full of phones

This is the whole manual. It explains what Deep-Guard is for and why each part exists, then walks you through setting it up on a Windows laptop and running the demo act by act, with what to click, what you will see and what to say. You don't need to know the project to follow it.

Every command and result on this page comes from a real dry run on 13 November 2026: a fresh clone of GitHub main (Stage 4), set up exactly as written here and clicked through in Microsoft Edge. The screenshots are from that run, so your screen should look the same.

Set up at home
About 25 min, needs internet (≈470 MB)
The night before
5 min, then Bitcoin works overnight
The demo
About 30 min, or a 5- or 10-minute version
Tested
112 ledger tests + 118 app tests pass on the fresh copy
How to use this page.
  1. Read Why Deep-Guard exists once, even if you skip everything else. It is the story your demo tells.
  2. Do At home the day before, with internet. Tick the checklist at the end.
  3. In class, follow In class and then The demo from top to bottom. Each step says what to do, what you'll see, and one thing to say.
1

Why Deep-Guard exists

5 min read

Anyone can make a convincing fake photo in seconds now, and fake photos of real people go round WhatsApp groups faster than anyone can check them. The usual answer is an AI detector: a program that looks at a picture and guesses whether a computer made it. Detectors are useful, but they are losing a race. Every new image generator leaves different traces, and a detector only knows the generators it was trained on.

We measured our own detector honestly, on 621 labelled pictures it had never seen:

34 of 34DALL·E 3 pictures caught. Generators it learned from, it catches.
58%of AI pictures caught overall. Newer generators slip past it.
14%of real photos wrongly flagged as AI. A guess can also accuse the innocent.

A guess is not good enough when someone's reputation depends on the answer. So Deep-Guard asks a different question first: where did this picture come from? If the person who made a photo wrote it down when they made it, nobody has to guess later. You only have to check the record. The detector still runs, but only for pictures nobody registered, and it is always labelled a guess.

The whole project in one line

“Detection guesses. Provenance proves. Deep-Guard checks the proof first, shows its work, and lets anyone verify it without trusting us.”

A passport for a photo

The easiest way to understand Deep-Guard is to think of a passport. A passport doesn't stop anyone from lying about who they are; it gives everyone a way to check. Every part of Deep-Guard is one piece of that passport system.

Deep-Guard, as a passport officeEach part, and what it would be at a border
Fingerprints Stage 2
The photo's biometrics. They recognise it again even after it has been re-saved, compressed or cropped.
The ledger Stage 3
The passport office's register: who registered this photo, and when. Pages are stamped so none can be swapped quietly.
The creator's signature Stage 3
The holder's own signature on the application, so nobody else can file in their name.
Witnesses Stage 3
Two independent notaries who keep their own copy of the register. If the office rewrites a page, their copies disagree.
The Bitcoin anchor Stage 4
A date stamp from the whole world's clock. Even the office and the notaries together can't backdate it.
The hidden ID Stage 4
A chip sewn into the photo itself. WhatsApp can tear off every label; the chip still says whose photo it is.
Content Credentials Stage 4
The international passport format. Other countries' border posts, here Adobe's and other apps, can read it.
Lens and the public link Stage 4
Border checks wherever photos turn up: one right-click on any website, or any phone in the room.
The AI detector Stage 1
The officer's hunch about a traveller with no passport at all. Worth hearing, never proof.

Every part closes one gap

The parts aren't a collection of features. Each one exists because the one before it left a question open. Read the table from top to bottom: that is also the order of the demo.

The question someone asksThe part that answers itShown in
1“Is this picture AI-made?”The detectorA trained neural network, with a heatmap of where it looked. It can only guess.Act 1
2“Is this the same photo, re-saved or cropped?”Three fingerprintsExact, look-alike and content fingerprints, each surviving a different change.Act 2, Act 4
3“Who made it, and when?”The ledgerRecords signed by their creator, sealed into a chain of signed blocks.Act 3
4“Couldn't the people running the ledger change it later?”WitnessesSeparate servers that keep their own copy of every block's fingerprint.Act 5
5“Couldn't they and the witnesses agree to backdate it?”The Bitcoin anchorThe block's fingerprint, written into Bitcoin, which nobody controls.Act 5
6“WhatsApp stripped everything. Whose photo is this?”The hidden IDAn invisible ID in the pixels of the copy you share.Act 4
7“Can other apps understand our label?”Content CredentialsThe industry's “CR” label, which Adobe, Google and OpenAI also use.Act 7
8“Do I have to come to your website to check?”Deep-Guard LensA browser extension: right-click any picture on any website.Act 8
9“Can I try it without installing anything?”The public linkA QR code on the projector; every phone in the room can use it.Act 9

The life of one photo

This is the path the demo follows, using a real family photo. Keep it in mind: every act is one stop on it.

  1. It is takenA photo of two children, on a family camera. Nothing special yet: just a file.
  2. Its creator registers itDeep-Guard takes its three fingerprints. The creator's own key signs the record. The picture itself is never stored. Act 3
  3. It gets a passport copyDeep-Guard hands back a “credentialed copy” that looks identical but carries a hidden ID in its pixels and a Content Credentials label. That is the copy to share. Act 3
  4. The record is sealed, witnessed and anchoredIt goes into a signed block, two witnesses co-sign it, and the block's fingerprint is written into Bitcoin. Act 5
  5. It travelsSomeone forwards it on WhatsApp, which shrinks it and strips every label; someone crops it; someone posts it online. Act 4
  6. Someone checks itOn the Ledger page, with a right-click on any website, or on their own phone. The hidden ID or the fingerprints lead back to the record, and the proof is re-checked in their own browser. Acts 4, 5, 8, 9
  7. And a picture nobody registered?Then there is no record, so Deep-Guard shows the detector's guess, with its heatmap, clearly labelled “a prediction, not proof”. Act 1

The four verdicts

Every check ends in one of four verdicts. Provenance comes first, and the prediction comes last:

Verdict 1Authentic & unalteredThe exact file is on the ledger, byte for byte.
Verdict 2Visually authentic, file modifiedThe same picture in a different file: re-saved, compressed or cropped.
Verdict 3No provenance foundNo record, so the AI detector runs, labelled a prediction.
Verdict 4Registered as AI-generatedIts creator declared it AI-made: honest synthetic content.
2

How each part works, in plain words

10 min read

Read this when you want to explain a part properly, or when the teacher asks “how does that work?”. Each card says what the part does, how it works, why it's there, and what it can't do.

The AI detector

Stage 1See it in Act 1
What it does
Says how likely it is that a picture or video was made or edited by AI, and shows its work.
How
An EfficientNet-B0 neural network we trained on hundreds of thousands of real and fake images. It shows four kinds of evidence: a heatmap of the regions that pushed it towards “AI” (Grad-CAM), a repeat check of how stable its answer is, a frequency picture of the pixels that needs no model at all, and on request a ranking of which regions mattered most (SHAP).
Why it's there
It is the only answer for a picture nobody registered.
Limits
It catches 58% of AI pictures from generators it never saw, and wrongly flags 14% of real photos. That is why it comes last.

Three fingerprints

Stage 2See them in Act 4
What they do
Recognise a picture again, each one through a different kind of change.
How
SHA-256 is a fingerprint of the exact bytes: change one byte and it changes completely, so it proves “this is the very same file”. pHash is a 256-bit sketch of what the picture looks like; a WhatsApp-style re-save moved it by 2 bits of 256. SSCD is Meta's copy-detection model; it recognises the same content even in a crop (0.80 similarity for our crop, where 0.40 counts as a match).
Why they're there
Real pictures get re-saved and cropped on their way round. A ledger that only knew exact files would lose them at the first forward.
Limits
pHash breaks under crops and SSCD can miss very small fragments, which is why there are three, plus the hidden ID.

The content registry

Stage 2See it in Act 2
What it does
Finds a disguised copy of a registered artwork, and explains why it matched.
How
SSCD finds the candidate; then hundreds of distinctive points (SIFT) that agree on one position confirm it and work out the edits: how much was cropped, whether it was mirrored, whether the colour was removed.
Why it's there
It shows that “the same picture” can be proved even after deliberate disguise.
Limits
It keeps no pictures, only points and numbers, and a fragment smaller than about a quarter can be missed.

The ledger

Stage 3See it in Act 3
What it does
Keeps a permanent, signed record of who registered which picture, when, and what they claimed it is.
How
A registration holds the three fingerprints, the creator's claim (camera original, edited, or AI-generated) and what the detector saw. The creator's own Ed25519 key signs it. Records are sealed into blocks; each block holds a summary of its records (a Merkle root) and the fingerprint of the block before it, and Deep-Guard signs it. Think of a notebook where every page is stamped with a summary of the page before: rewrite one old page and every stamp after it stops matching.
Why it's there
It turns “I think this is real” into “here is the record, check it yourself”.
Limits
It proves who wrote a picture down first, not who really took it. Disputes exist for that. Creators' keys are kept by the server (a simulated setup, see Questions).

Witnesses

Stage 3See them in Act 5
What they do
Stop Deep-Guard itself from rewriting history.
How
Two separate programs, each with its own key and its own notebook, receive every new block, check it, write down its fingerprint and co-sign it. If Deep-Guard ever shows them a different version of an old block, they refuse and raise an alarm.
Why they're there
Deep-Guard holds the key that signs blocks, so on its own it could re-sign a rewritten history perfectly. Certificate Transparency, which keeps the padlock in your browser honest, works the same way.
Limits
In the demo they run on the same laptop. Real witnesses would be other people's computers; that is the next step of the project.

The Bitcoin anchor

Stage 4See it in Act 5
What it does
Proves that a block existed, exactly as it is, by a certain date, using a clock nobody controls.
How
Deep-Guard sends the block's fingerprint to the free OpenTimestamps calendars. They combine many people's fingerprints into one Bitcoin transaction. Once a Bitcoin block includes it (usually within a few hours), anyone can follow 79 small hashing steps from our block to that Bitcoin block's own summary. Like printing a sealed fingerprint in the world's most-watched newspaper: nobody can reprint yesterday's paper.
Why it's there
Deep-Guard and its witnesses together could still agree to rewrite the past. Bitcoin is run by thousands of strangers.
Limits
It costs nothing and buys no cryptocurrency, but it needs internet and time to confirm. Only the fingerprint leaves the laptop.

The hidden ID

Stage 4See it in Act 4
What it does
Lets a copy point home after WhatsApp, Instagram or a screenshot has thrown away every label.
How
At registration Deep-Guard hides a random 61-bit ID in the pixels of a credentialed copy, using TrustMark, Adobe Research's open watermark. It is invisible. Reading the pixels of a later copy gives the ID back, and the ID names the record. In our measurements it survived a WhatsApp-style re-save, an 80% crop sent through WhatsApp, and a screenshot, on all 55 test pictures.
Why it's there
Messaging apps strip metadata and re-compress, which is exactly when people most need to know where a picture came from.
Limits
An ID only counts if the picture's content also matches the record, so it can't be lifted onto another picture. TrustMark's own remover can erase it; the fingerprints are the fallback.

Content Credentials

Stage 4See them in Act 7
What they do
Put a signed label inside the file that other apps understand: who made it, with what, what was done to it, and whether AI made it.
How
C2PA is the standard behind the small “CR” mark, used by Adobe, Google, OpenAI, LinkedIn and several camera makers. Deep-Guard reads the label on every file it checks (testing the signer against the official trust lists) and writes one into the credentialed copy. Adobe's own checker reads ours.
Why they're there
A provenance system that only it can read helps nobody. This one speaks the industry's language.
Limits
Our signing certificate comes from a student demo authority, so other tools show the label but call the issuer “unrecognized”. A re-save strips the label, which is why the hidden ID and fingerprints exist.

The Explorer, receipts and the offline checker

Stage 3See them in Act 5
What they do
Let anyone check everything without trusting the Deep-Guard server.
How
The Explorer recomputes every hash, Merkle root and signature in your own browser, asks the witnesses directly and replays the Bitcoin proof itself. A receipt is a small file that proves one record with no server at all, and tools/verify_ledger.py checks the whole chain with only Python. A tamper lab runs five attacks on a copy of the chain so you can watch them get caught.
Why they're there
“Trust us” is the problem Deep-Guard is meant to solve, so it must not ask for it.

Deep-Guard Lens

Stage 4See it in Act 8
What it does
Checks a picture where you find it: right-click it on any website and choose Check with Deep-Guard.
How
A small extension for Edge and Chrome. It downloads the picture, asks your Deep-Guard server, and pins a badge on the picture with the verdict, the record, how it matched and the Content Credentials. It decides nothing itself.
Why it's there
Nobody visits a provenance website before believing a photo. The check has to come to the picture.
Limits
Loaded by hand as a developer extension (not from the store), and it only sees normal pictures, not ones drawn on a canvas.

The public link and QR code

Stage 4See it in Act 9
What it does
Lets everyone in the room use the real Deep-Guard on their own phone, with nothing to install.
How
run_deepguard.py --public starts a free Cloudflare “quick tunnel”: the laptop calls Cloudflare and keeps the line open, and visitors' requests come back down it. The college network never has to let anyone in. A QR code on the projector carries the link. Visitors get fair-use limits, can't use the owner's actions, and can't take the laptop's creator names.
Why it's there
Seeing it work on your own phone is more convincing than watching a demo.
Limits
Needs internet; the link changes every time and dies when you press Ctrl+C. Cloudflare gives quick tunnels no uptime guarantee.
3

At home, the day before

≈25 min · needs internet

Do all of this on the laptop you will present from. Every command goes into Windows PowerShell: press Start, type PowerShell, press Enter. Run the boxes one at a time, in order. Each Copy button copies one command; paste it with a right-click or Ctrl+V and press Enter.

1

Check that Python and Git are installed

python --version
git --version
You should see Python 3.11 up to 3.14 (the dry run used 3.13.7) and git version 2.something.

If python opens the Microsoft Store or isn't found, install Python 3.13 from python.org, tick “Add python.exe to PATH” on the first screen, then close and reopen PowerShell. If git isn't found, install Git for Windows from git-scm.com.

2

Download the project from GitHub

This puts it in your home folder (C:\Users\<you>\deep_guard). Keep the path short: Windows refuses file paths over 260 characters, and one file inside PyTorch is 141 characters on its own.

cd $HOME
git clone https://github.com/rabdeepsinghdhaliwal/deep_guard.git
cd deep_guard
git log --oneline -1
You should see the newest commit, which adds this runbook, or anything newer. The clone took 17 seconds in the dry run and takes 277 MB, because the trained models are inside the repository.

Already have the folder from before? Delete it and clone again. A copy made before this commit has a few test files with the wrong line endings (see If it breaks).

3

Make the virtual environment and install the packages

Still inside deep_guard. A virtual environment (“venv”) is a private folder of Python packages just for this project. The second line lets this one PowerShell window run the venv's activation script; it changes nothing permanently and needs no admin rights.

python -m venv deepguard-bouncer\venv
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force
.\deepguard-bouncer\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r deepguard-bouncer\app\requirements.txt
pip install -r deepguard-ledger\requirements.txt
pip install pytest httpx
You should see (venv) at the start of the prompt after the third line, and each install ending with Successfully installed …. The first install is the detector's (about 300 MB, PyTorch included); the second adds Stage 4's packages (about 95 MB: Bitcoin timestamps, the hidden ID, Content Credentials, QR codes). The last line adds the test runner, for showing the tests live. The dry run took 7 minutes; on slow Wi-Fi allow 15–20.
4

Put every demo file into one demo folder

This copies the pictures you will use into one place and makes three edited copies: a re-saved JPEG, a crop, and a cropped, mirrored, black-and-white Mona Lisa. Everything you upload in class then comes from deep_guard\demo.

mkdir demo
Copy-Item test_images\real1.png, test_images\real2.jpg, test_images\real3.jpg, test_images\real4.jpg, test_images\ai1.png, generalization_test\held_out_images\dalle3\dalle3_000.webp, generalization_test\held_out_images\dalle3\dalle3_002.webp demo
python -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('demo/real3.jpg').save('demo/family_resaved.jpg', quality=60)"
python -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('demo/real3.jpg').crop((0, 0, 1300, 1500)).save('demo/family_cropped.jpg')"
python -c "from PIL import Image, ImageOps; im = Image.open('deepguard-bouncer/demo_artworks/mona_lisa.jpg'); w, h = im.size; ImageOps.mirror(ImageOps.grayscale(im.crop((w//5, h//8, w*4//5, h*5//8)))).save('demo/mona_copy.jpg')"
dir demo
You should see ten files in demo. One more, the WhatsApp copy, is made during the demo (step 16).
FileWhat it isUsed in
dalle3_000.webpAn avocado on a therapist's couch, from OpenAI's DALL·E 3 examplesStep 8 (registered the night before), verdict 4
dalle3_002.webpA porcelain dancer, DALL·E 3, never registeredAct 1, verdict 3, Act 8
real3.jpgA real family photo of two childrenActs 1, 3, 4, 8
family_resaved.jpgThe same photo re-saved as JPEG quality 60Extra verdict 2
family_cropped.jpgThe left 65% of the same photoVerdict 2 by content
mona_copy.jpgMona Lisa's face: cropped, mirrored and made black-and-whiteAct 2
real1.png, real2.jpg, real4.jpgTwo portraits and a school photoSpare pictures
ai1.pngAn AI-made hiker in stock-photo style that the detector missesOnly if asked about weaknesses
5

Start it once, and let it download the hidden-ID model

cd deepguard-ledger
python run_deepguard.py

Wait for Application startup complete (40 seconds the very first time in the dry run). Then keep waiting for this line:

INFO:deepguard:Hidden-ID model (TrustMark Q) ready in 152 s

The very first start downloads the hidden-ID model (about 65 MB, from Adobe's server). It took 2½ minutes in the dry run, and only happens once: later starts say ready in 3 s. Meanwhile, open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in Edge or Chrome: the pill at the top right should say Ready with a green dot. Leave the server running for steps 6 to 8.

Don't skip the wait

If the model never downloads and there is no internet in class, registering still works, but the copies get no hidden ID, and Act 4's best moment disappears.

Also normal on a fresh copy
  • Yellow FutureWarning: `torch.jit.load` is deprecated lines. They are harmless.
  • No concept labeler in models/. The optional 605 MB “namer” isn't built, so the registry names areas by position (“top left area”). Leave it off.
  • git status now shows demo_signer_public.pem as changed. Every installation makes its own signing key on first start. Don't commit it.
6

Install the Deep-Guard Lens extension

  1. In Edge, type edge://extensions in the address bar and press Enter. (Chrome: chrome://extensions.)
  2. Switch on Developer mode: bottom left in Edge, top right in Chrome.
  3. Click Load unpacked and choose the folder C:\Users\<you>\deep_guard\deepguard-lens.
  4. Click the puzzle-piece button in the toolbar and pin Deep-Guard Lens, so its shield shows.
  5. Click the shield. With the server running it says Connected.
7

Get cloudflared, for the public link optional

Only needed for Act 9. cloudflared is Cloudflare's free tunnel program: one file, about 55 MB, signed by Cloudflare, Inc., no account needed. Pick one way:

  • Easiest: run the line below, then close PowerShell and open a new window, so it can find the program.
winget install --id Cloudflare.cloudflared
  • Or by hand: from github.com/cloudflare/cloudflared/releases, download cloudflared-windows-amd64.exe and save it as deep_guard\deepguard-ledger\tools\cloudflared.exe. Git ignores it there.
8

The night before: reset the ledger and anchor yesterday's picture

Bitcoin takes from a few minutes to a few hours to confirm an anchor, so you prepare one block the night before (at least 6 hours ahead). In class you'll show it already sealed into Bitcoin, and register everything else live.

  1. Stop the server: click its PowerShell window and press Ctrl+C. Then reset the ledger, which deletes only the ledger's own data (blocks, witness notebooks, creator keys):
cd $HOME\deep_guard
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force deepguard-ledger\ledger_data -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
cd deepguard-ledger
python run_deepguard.py
  1. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ledger. Under Register a file: file demo\dalle3_000.webp, title Avocado therapist (DALL-E 3), creator Arjun, and choose AI-generated (declared). Click Register on the ledger. It says Written to block #1.
  2. In the box under it, click Download dalle3_000.credentialed.jpg. Edge saves it to Downloads; you'll use it in Act 7.
  3. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/explorer, scroll to Anchored in Bitcoin and click Anchor block #1 to Bitcoin.

You can stop the server now. The calendars do the waiting, not your laptop.

Why this matters

This is the one step that can't be rushed: nobody, including you, can put a fingerprint into an old Bitcoin block. That is exactly what makes it proof.

9

The morning of the demo: check Bitcoin

With internet, start the server (as in step 8), open the Explorer, and click Check for Bitcoin confirmation. Block #1 should now say ✓ In Bitcoin block #… with the date it was mined.

If it still says Waiting for Bitcoin, that's normal on a slow day. Show it as “waiting” in class and explain; the tamper-lab attack in step 19 still works, because the calendars already hold the fingerprint. Don't reset the ledger again: that would delete the anchored block.

Ready for class when…

Presenting from a Mac or Linux laptop instead?

Same steps with Unix commands: python3 -m venv deepguard-bouncer/venv, then source deepguard-bouncer/venv/bin/activate, then the three pip install lines with forward slashes. On Linux run pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu first, or pip fetches a multi-gigabyte GPU build. For step 4 use mkdir demo and cp with forward slashes; the python -c lines work as written. Reset with rm -rf deepguard-ledger/ledger_data. cloudflared comes from your package manager or Cloudflare's releases page. This path was not part of the dry run.

4

In class: start Deep-Guard

2 min before you begin
10

Start the server, the two witnesses and (with internet) the public link

Open a fresh PowerShell window:

cd $HOME\deep_guard
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force
.\deepguard-bouncer\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
cd deepguard-ledger

With internet, start it with the public link, so Act 9 needs no restart:

python run_deepguard.py --public

Without internet, start it plainly. Everything works except anchoring a new block, Act 7's website and Act 9:

python run_deepguard.py

Leave this window open for the whole demo. It is the server, and it logs every click. The public link works until you press Ctrl+C in it.

11

Open the pages and the demo folder

In Edge or Chrome open http://127.0.0.1:8000 and wait for Ready. Also open File Explorer at C:\Users\<you>\deep_guard\demo. You can drag files from there onto the page, or, in the browser's file picker, paste %USERPROFILE%\deep_guard\demo into the File name box and press Enter. Keep a second PowerShell window ready for steps 16, 21 and 23.

Pick your pictures on purpose

Use the DALL·E pictures for “AI” and real3.jpg for “real”. These come out wrong, so don't use them as examples:

  • test_images\ai1.png, ai2.png and ai3.png are AI pictures the detector calls authentic. ai4.png and real2.jpg come out inconclusive.
  • The three paintings in demo_artworks are real, but the detector calls them AI-generated. Paintings aren't photos.

If the teacher hands you a picture of their own, say up front that the detector is a guess. That is the reason the rest of Deep-Guard exists.

5

The demo

≈30 min, nine acts

Nine acts, from the guess to the proof to the room. Each act opens with the question it answers, then gives the steps: what to click, what appears, and one thing to say. Steps marked optional can be skipped without breaking later ones.

Only 5 minutes?

  1. Step 12: the detector says 100% AI
  2. Step 15: register the family photo
  3. Steps 16–17: only the WhatsApp copy, found by its hidden ID
  4. Step 19: attacks 4 and 5, then the Bitcoin anchor
  5. Step 28: the QR code, if you have internet

Only 10 minutes?

  1. The five above, plus:
  2. Step 17: all six verdicts
  3. Step 20: Bitcoin, checked from the browser
  4. Step 26: Lens on a real website
Act 1

The detector guesses

Analysis page · 3 min

The question: “Is this picture AI-made?” Start with what everyone expects from a deepfake tool, then show why it isn't enough.

12

Analyse an AI picture: demo\dalle3_002.webp

On http://127.0.0.1:8000, drop the file on the box (or click it and browse), then click Analyse this image. It took 2.3 seconds in the dry run.

Scroll down through the panels: the frequency signature (evidence from the pixels with no model involved), “Can't tell which tool made this” (the tool-naming model is switched off because it was unreliable), the signed fingerprint, and at the very bottom the provenance card:

Optional: Test compression resilience

Click Test compression resilience in the fingerprint panel. The exact fingerprint changes at every JPEG quality, while the look-alike fingerprint moves 0 bits of 256.

Say

“Our detector says 100% AI and shows where it looked. But a detector is only a guess: on generators it has never seen, it catches 58% of fakes. So before it trusts the guess, Deep-Guard asks a better question at the bottom: did anyone register this picture? Nobody did.”

13

Analyse a real photo: demo\real3.jpg

Click Choose a different file, pick real3.jpg, click Analyse this image.

Act 2

Recognising a copy

Registry page · 2 min · optional

The question: “Is this the same picture, even disguised?” Fingerprints are what let the ledger follow a picture after it changes.

14

Check a disguised Mona Lisa: demo\mona_copy.jpg

Click Registry in the menu. The three paintings were registered automatically on first start. Under Check for copies, choose mona_copy.jpg and click Check registry.

Say

“We cropped it, flipped it and made it black and white. Meta's copy-detection model still finds it, and 265 points that agree on one position prove it. The registry never keeps the picture itself.”

Act 3

Writing it down

Ledger page · 3 min

The question: “Who made this, and when?” This is the moment the photo gets its passport.

15

Register the family photo, and download its credentialed copy

Click Ledger in the menu. Under Register a file:

Filedemo\real3.jpg
TitleFamily photo (exactly this: step 21 searches for it)
Your creator nameRabdeep (any name works; use the same one again in step 30)
What is this file?Camera original
Seal into a new block right awayleave it ticked

Click Register on the ledger (1.9 seconds in the dry run). Then click Download real3.credentialed.jpg in the box that appears. Edge saves it to your Downloads folder.

Say

“The record holds three fingerprints, Rabdeep's claim that it's a camera original, and what the detector saw. Rabdeep's own key signs it, Deep-Guard seals it into block #2, and two independent witnesses co-sign. The photo itself is never stored. And we get back a credentialed copy: it looks identical, but it carries an invisible ID in its pixels and a Content Credentials label. That's the copy you'd share.”

Act 4

The copies come back

Ledger page · 5 min

The question: “WhatsApp stripped everything. Whose photo is this?” Six files come back to the ledger; each gets the verdict it deserves.

16

Make a WhatsApp copy of the credentialed copy

The real way needs internet: send real3.credentialed.jpg to yourself on WhatsApp, save the received photo, and put it in the demo folder as family_whatsapp.jpg.

The offline way, which does what WhatsApp does (longest side 1600 pixels, JPEG quality 75, every label removed; the same squeeze our measurements used). In your second PowerShell window:

cd $HOME\deep_guard
$c = (Get-ChildItem $HOME\Downloads\real3.credentialed*.jpg | Sort-Object LastWriteTime | Select-Object -Last 1).FullName
.\deepguard-bouncer\venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; from PIL import Image; im = Image.open(sys.argv[1]); im.thumbnail((1600, 1600)); im.save('demo/family_whatsapp.jpg', quality=75)" $c
You should see no output. A new family_whatsapp.jpg (173 KB in the dry run, 1600 × 1200) appears in the demo folder.

19

Tamper lab: five attacks, each one harder to catch

Scroll to Tamper lab. Pick an attack and a block, click Run the attack. The attacks run on a copy of the chain; the real files are never touched.

AttackBlockResult in the dry run
1 · Edit an old record#2Caught by the chain itself at block #2: the records no longer match the Merkle root.
2 · Edit it and recompute the hashes, without the key#2Caught at block #2: the old signature doesn't fit the new hash.
3 · Delete a block#1Caught at block #1: the numbering and the link break.
4 · Insider rewrite with the real key#2“The rewritten chain checks out perfectly on its own — only the witnesses catch it, because their copies still hold the original hashes.”
5 · Collusion: the witnesses go along too#2“Nothing catches this one yet: no anchor covers the rewritten blocks.”
5 · Collusion#1“Only the anchor of block #1 catches it”: the hash written into Bitcoin no longer matches.

Close the gap live needs internet: scroll up to Anchored in Bitcoin, click Anchor block #2 to Bitcoin, then run attack 5 on block #2 again.

Say

“Attack 4: Deep-Guard itself rewrites history with its real key. The chain looks perfect, but the witnesses kept their own copies. Attack 5: now the witnesses are in on it too, and nothing inside the system can catch it. Only something outside can. Last night we wrote block #1's fingerprint into Bitcoin, and nobody can rewrite Bitcoin. Watch: I anchor block #2 now, and the same attack is caught.”

6

How ordinary people could use this

Deep-Guard is a student project, but every part of it mirrors something the real world is starting to build. This is where it leads, if the pieces are joined up.

Your camera registers the photo the moment you take it

Some cameras and phones already sign photos with Content Credentials at capture: Leica, Sony and Nikon cameras, and Google's recent Pixel phones. Add a registration step and every photo would have a passport from its first second, before anyone could fake it.

Deep-Guard parts: registration, Content Credentials, the hidden ID

A check button on every forwarded picture

Imagine Lens built into WhatsApp: a forwarded photo shows “Registered by the Times of India, 3 Nov” or “No record anywhere; the AI detector thinks 92%, which is a guess”. The hidden ID survives the forwarding that strips everything else.

Lens, the hidden ID, the four verdicts

Fake circulars and fake news photos fail instantly

Schools, colleges, newspapers and governments register what they publish. A fake “school closed tomorrow” notice, or a news photo with a newspaper's logo pasted on, simply has no record, or matches a record that says something different.

The ledger, fingerprints, the registry

Your family photos, protected

Register your own photos. If someone makes a deepfake from one, your record, stamped into Bitcoin on a date nobody can change, shows the original came first and what it really looked like.

The ledger, the Bitcoin anchor, disputes

Evidence that stays evidence

Insurance claims, police reports and court cases need to know a photo hasn't changed since a date. A receipt and a Bitcoin anchor prove it to anyone, offline, without trusting the company that stored it.

Receipts, the offline checker, the Bitcoin anchor

Elections and emergencies

Official pictures and videos from the Election Commission or disaster agencies are registered as they're released. An edited version gets verdict 2 (“same picture, file modified”) instead of being mistaken for the original.

The ledger, witnesses run by independent groups

What it would take

  • Creators hold their own keys, on their phone or camera, instead of the server keeping them.
  • Witnesses run by independent organisations on their own computers. Running them on three friends' laptops is the project's next step.
  • A certificate on the official C2PA trust list, so other apps show “recognised” instead of “unrecognized”.
  • Checks built into the apps people already use, so nobody needs an extension or a QR code.
  • A detector trained on many more generators, for the pictures nobody registered.
7

If the teacher asks

Short, true answers. The numbers come from the project's own measurements.

Is this a blockchain?

It uses a blockchain's data structure: hash-linked blocks, Merkle trees and digital signatures, with no mining, tokens or currency of its own. We don't need strangers to agree with each other; we need a record nobody can change quietly. The witnesses provide that, the way Certificate Transparency logs do for HTTPS certificates. For the one thing witnesses can't guarantee, that nobody colluded, we use the biggest public blockchain, Bitcoin, purely as a clock.

Did you buy Bitcoin? Does anchoring cost money?

No and no. OpenTimestamps is a free public service: its calendars combine thousands of fingerprints into one Bitcoin transaction and pay for it themselves. We send only a 32-byte fingerprint of a block, never a picture. The proof can then be checked by anyone, with our explorer, with our offline tool, or on opentimestamps.org.

What stops Deep-Guard itself from cheating?

Two layers. The witnesses: separate processes with their own keys and notebooks. Tamper-lab attack 4 shows Deep-Guard re-signing a rewritten history with its real key; the chain passes every check, and both witnesses still catch it. And Bitcoin: attack 5 has the witnesses collude too, and only the Bitcoin anchor catches it.

Do you store people's photos?

No. Only fingerprints: the SHA-256, the 256-bit pHash, and the hash of the 512-number SSCD vector (the vector itself is kept beside the ledger so crops can be matched). The credentialed copy is handed back once and never stored. On the public link, checked pictures are processed and forgotten.

Why three different fingerprints, and a hidden ID?

Each survives a different change. SHA-256 changes if one byte changes, so it proves the exact file. The pHash survives re-compression (our re-save changed 2 of 256 bits) but breaks under cropping. SSCD survives crops (0.80, threshold 0.40). The hidden ID survives all of them together, and screenshots, because it is in the pixels themselves, and it points straight at one record instead of searching.

Can the hidden ID be removed or faked?

Removed, yes: TrustMark ships a remover model, and anyone with it can strip the mark. Then Deep-Guard falls back to the fingerprints. Faked, no: an ID only counts if the picture's content also matches the record it names, so copying an ID onto another picture is caught, and the page says so. A test pins exactly that case.

Why does Adobe's site say “Unrecognized”?

Content Credentials are trusted when the signing certificate comes from a member of the C2PA conformance programme. Ours comes from a certificate authority Deep-Guard makes for itself, which is right for a student demo. Adobe's checker still reads everything inside correctly, including “generated with an AI tool”. Deep-Guard itself checks other files against the two official trust lists.

How accurate is the AI detector?

On its own test split it scored 98.17%, but most of those fakes were one kind of face, so we built a harder exam: 621 labelled images it had never seen, many from newer generators. There it catches 58% of AI images, with 14% false alarms on real photos. It catches DALL·E 3 every time (34 of 34) and is weakest on the newest generators and on polished stock-photo styles. That is why the ledger checks provenance first and labels the detector's reading “a prediction, not proof”. To show a miss honestly, analyse demo\ai1.png: an AI-made hiker that the detector calls authentic.

Who checks that a creator is who they claim?

Nobody yet, and the code says so. It's a simulated public-key setup: the server keeps creators' keys, like a custodial wallet. A real system needs creators to hold their own keys and a certificate authority to vouch for them, which is still an open problem even for C2PA. The ledger proves who wrote a picture down first, not who really took it.

What if someone registers my photo before me?

First registration wins, and the real owner files a dispute. Deep-Guard writes its decision as a resolution record. Only the original creator can revoke a registration; step 30 shows someone else being refused.

Is the public link safe for the laptop?

Visitors reach only Deep-Guard's own pages, not the laptop's files. They get upload and speed limits, can't use the owner's actions, can't take the laptop's creator names, and the witnesses refuse anything sent through the link. The link is a random address that stops working the moment you press Ctrl+C. All of these rules have tests.

Why are the witnesses on the same laptop?

To demonstrate the mechanism. They are separate processes on ports 8101 and 8102, with separate keys and files. Real witnesses would be run by other organisations on other machines; running them on three friends' laptops is the next planned step.

Which parts did you build, and which did you use?

We fine-tuned the EfficientNet-B0 detector and trained the generator-attribution model ourselves in Colab. We wrote the fingerprinting, the registry and its explanations, the evaluation exam, the ledger, the witnesses, the Explorer, the offline checkers, the Bitcoin anchoring, the hidden-ID and Content Credentials integration, the public-link rules and the Lens extension. We used: Meta's SSCD copy-detection model, Adobe Research's TrustMark watermark, the C2PA project's official library, the OpenTimestamps library and calendars, Cloudflare's tunnel program, and libraries such as PyTorch, FastAPI, FAISS and cryptography.

Does it work on video?

Yes. The analysis samples up to 32 frames across the whole clip and shows a timeline, and the ledger stores one look-alike fingerprint per sampled frame. Trimmed or re-timed clips may not match, and videos get no hidden ID; the README lists both as limits.

How do you know it works?

112 ledger tests (the maths and every attack, Bitcoin anchors against the official OpenTimestamps example and our real proof, Content Credentials against the official C2PA test files, the hidden ID, the public link's rules, and the whole app with real models and witness servers) and 118 detector tests. And this page: a fresh copy, set up from GitHub and clicked through act by act. That dry run found and fixed a real bug: Git on Windows was changing the line endings of one test file, which broke three tests on every fresh copy.

8

If something breaks

What you seeWhat to do
python opens the Microsoft StoreInstall Python 3.13 from python.org with “Add python.exe to PATH” ticked, then reopen PowerShell.
git is not recognizedInstall Git for Windows. Or, on the GitHub page, use Code → Download ZIP, extract it into your home folder and rename deep_guard-main to deep_guard.
Clone fails with Filename too longThe folder path is too deep. Run git config --global core.longpaths true and clone into a short folder such as C:\dg.
running scripts is disabled on this systemRun the Set-ExecutionPolicy … -Force line again. Every new PowerShell window needs it once.
Hidden-ID model unavailable, so registrations get no hidden IDThe first start had no internet, so the model couldn't download. Connect, stop the server and start it again; wait for “Hidden-ID model … ready”.
3 tests fail with the proof was made for different bytes, or git status shows test fixture files as changedYour copy was cloned before the fix for Windows line endings. From deep_guard, after git pull, run Remove-Item -Recurse -Force deepguard-ledger\tests\fixtures and then git restore deepguard-ledger/tests/fixtures. Git puts every file back with its exact bytes.
Browser: “can't reach this page”, or the pill says “Service offline”The server window was closed or is still loading. Wait for Application startup complete, or start it again (step 10).
error while attempting to bind on address ('127.0.0.1', 8000)An old copy is still running. Close other PowerShell windows; if it persists, run taskkill /F /IM python.exe (it closes every Python program) and start again.
Ledger or Explorer page says “Not Found”The old detector-only server was started (uvicorn main:app). Stop it and start python run_deepguard.py from deepguard-ledger.
The Explorer shows a witness “did not answer”The witnesses didn't start, usually because an old copy still holds port 8101 or 8102. Stop everything, run taskkill /F /IM python.exe, and start again.
“This exact file is already registered…” at step 15The ledger still holds an earlier test. Use it as the “first registration wins” moment, or reset the ledger (step 8) and redo the night-before steps.
Block #1 still says “Waiting for Bitcoin” in classNormal on a slow day. Show it as pending; attack 5 on block #1 is still caught, by the calendars. Anchor earlier next time.
“Anchor block … to Bitcoin” failsNo internet: the calendars can't be reached. Skip the live anchoring; everything else works.
The Explorer says “tampered” when you didn't mean itchain.jsonl still has your edit. Undo it in Notepad and save.
“Line N of chain.jsonl is not valid JSON”A quote or bracket was deleted while editing. Ctrl+Z until it's back, then save.
Lens badge: “no Deep-Guard server answered at http://127.0.0.1:8000”Start the server. If it is running, click the shield and check the server address is http://127.0.0.1:8000.
No “Check with Deep-Guard” on right-clickRight-click the picture itself, not the space around it. Some sites draw pictures as backgrounds, which can't be checked. Check the extension is switched on in edge://extensions.
Lens: “This page doesn't allow extensions”Browser pages and the extension store block all extensions. Use a normal website.
--public needs cloudflaredDo step 7. After a winget install, open a new PowerShell window first.
The public link could not be openedThe network blocks Cloudflare's tunnel port (7844). Connect the laptop to a phone hotspot and start again.
A phone shows a Cloudflare error pageThe link isn't ready yet, or the server was stopped. Wait for “The public link is live”, or start again: the link will be new, so reload /share.
A visitor sees “That's a lot of checks in a minute”The fair-use limit. Wait 30 seconds.
A visitor sees “That creator name already belongs to someone on this laptop”Names used on the laptop are reserved. Pick another name.
Registry areas say “top left area” instead of “face”Normal on a fresh copy: the optional namer isn't built.
Fonts look plain in classNo internet, so the web fonts didn't load. Everything still works.

After the demo

Press Ctrl+C in the server window. It prints Closed the public link. (if it was open) and Stopped Deep-Guard and its witnesses. The public address stops working immediately. git status will show deepguard-bouncer/models/demo_signer_public.pem as changed and demo/ as new; leave both and don't commit them, because the changed key would stop the original server's signatures from verifying. You can delete the .credentialed.jpg files and receipts from Downloads. To run the demo again from the start, repeat step 8.

9

Words you'll hear

Provenance
Where something came from and what happened to it since. Deep-Guard's whole idea: check provenance first, guess last.
Hash, SHA-256
A fixed-length fingerprint of any data. Change one byte and the hash changes completely; nobody can find two files with the same one.
pHash
A “perceptual” hash: a 256-bit sketch of what a picture looks like, so similar-looking pictures get similar hashes.
SSCD
Meta's self-supervised copy-detection model. It turns a picture into 512 numbers that stay close even after crops and edits.
Ledger, block
The ledger is the append-only record. A block is one sealed page of it: some records, the previous block's hash, and Deep-Guard's signature.
Merkle tree, Merkle root
A way to summarise many records in one hash (the root), so that proving one record is inside needs only a few hashes, not all the records.
Signature, key pair, Ed25519
A private key signs; the matching public key lets anyone check the signature. Ed25519 is the signature scheme used throughout.
Witness, co-signature
A separate server that keeps its own copy of every block's hash and signs a statement “I saw block #N with this hash”.
Anchor, OpenTimestamps, calendar
An anchor ties a block's hash to a Bitcoin block. OpenTimestamps is the free service that does it; its calendars collect hashes and put their summary into Bitcoin.
Hidden ID, watermark, TrustMark
An invisible 61-bit ID in a picture's pixels. TrustMark is the open watermark from Adobe Research that hides and reads it.
Credentialed copy
The copy Deep-Guard hands back at registration: the same picture, with a hidden ID and a Content Credentials label. The one to share.
Content Credentials, C2PA
The industry standard (the “CR” mark) for a signed label inside a file: who made it, how, and whether AI was used.
Trust list, certificate authority
A certificate authority vouches for a signer. A trust list says which authorities a checker believes.
Detector, Grad-CAM
The neural network that guesses “AI or real”. Grad-CAM draws the heatmap of where it looked.
Verdict
One of the four answers: 1 exact file, 2 same picture in a modified file, 3 no record (only a guess), 4 declared AI.
Receipt
A small file proving one record is in one signed block, checkable offline.
Tamper lab
The Explorer's section that runs five attacks on a copy of the chain to show what catches each one.
Extension, Lens
A small add-on for the browser. Deep-Guard Lens adds “Check with Deep-Guard” to the right-click menu of pictures.
Quick tunnel, cloudflared
A free, temporary public address from Cloudflare. cloudflared is the program on the laptop that keeps the tunnel open.
Virtual environment, venv
A private folder of Python packages for one project, so it can't clash with anything else on the laptop.
Dry run: 13 November 2026 on Windows 11, Python 3.13.7, PyTorch 2.15.0 (CPU), Microsoft Edge 157, from a fresh clone of rabdeepsinghdhaliwal/deep_guard (Stage 4) plus the two fixes committed with this runbook. The step 20 screenshot comes from the project's own demo ledger (anchored 4 November 2026); the phone screenshots come from the same server in public mode. Your hashes, keys, IDs and timestamps will differ; the verdicts, matches and numbers should not.
